questions.question: In a periodic-review inventory system with a positive lead time, an $(s,S)$ policy with integers $s<S$ looks at the end-of-period inventory position $P_{k-1}'$ of period $k-1$. When does it place an order at the start of period $k$?
options: Whenever the stock on hand is at or below $s$

questions.question: In a periodic-review inventory system with a positive lead time, an $(s,S)$ policy orders $Q_k=(S-P_{k-1}')\,\mathbf{1}\{P_{k-1}'\le s\}$ at the start of period $k$, where $P_{k-1}'$ is the end-of-period inventory position of period $k-1$. What does the parameter $S$ represent?
options: The size of every order that is placed
The inventory position right after any order
The stock on the shelf right after any order
The largest position that still triggers an order

questions.question: In a periodic-review inventory system every order costs a fixed setup cost $K$, whatever its size. Why does an $(s,S)$ policy with a wide gap $S-s$ suit this better than reordering each period's demand at once?
options: It bundles several periods of demand into one order
It reduces the setup cost $K$ charged per order
It keeps the position at $S$, so no stock is held
It rules out backlog, since the position stays above $s$

questions.question: A base-stock policy with level $S$ orders $Q_k=S-P_{k-1}'$ at the start of every period $k$, where $P_{k-1}'\le S$ is the end-of-period inventory position. Which $(s,S)$ policy, ordering $(S-P_{k-1}')\,\mathbf{1}\{P_{k-1}'\le s\}$ with integer positions, places exactly the same orders?
options: $s=S-2$: a demand of two units is needed to trigger
$s=0$: an order follows when the position runs out
No $s<S$ works, as $(s,S)$ waits for demand to pass $s$

questions.question: Inventory policies differ in what they fix in advance: the order epochs (the periods in which orders are placed) and the order sizes. Which describes an $(s,S)$ policy with reorder level $s$ and order-up-to level $S$?
options: Orders follow a timetable, but their sizes vary
Every order has one size, placed at random times
Neither is fixed; both depend on the demands
Both are fixed once $s$ and $S$ are chosen

questions.question: An $(s,S)$ policy with $s=3$ and $S=10$ orders $S-P'$ when the end-of-period inventory position satisfies $P'\le s$, and nothing otherwise. A period ends with $P'=1$. How many units are ordered?

An $(s,S)$ policy with $s=5$ and $S=12$ orders $S-P'$ when the end-of-period inventory position satisfies $P'\le s$, and nothing otherwise. A period ends with $P'=5$ exactly. What is ordered, and what is the position just after ordering?
options: $7$ units, but the position waits for the delivery

questions.question: Two $(s,S)$ policies start at inventory position $9$, and demands in periods $1$ to $5$ are $2,1,4,0,2$. Each places an order at the start of period $k\in\{2,\dots,6\}$ if the end-of-period position $P_{k-1}'\le s$, raising it to $S=9$. How many orders do the $(3,9)$ policy and the base-stock policy $(8,9)$ place?

A simulation of an $(s,S)$ policy over $12$ periods charges setup cost $K=20$ per order and holding cost $h=1$ per unit on hand at the start of each period. It places $4$ orders, the start-of-period on-hand levels sum to $55$, and no backlog occurs. What is the average cost per period?

An $(s,S)$ policy with $s=4$ and $S=9$ starts period $1$ at inventory position $P_1=9$. It orders $S-P_{k-1}'$ at the start of period $k$ if the end-of-period position $P_{k-1}'\le s$. Demands are $D_1=3$ and $D_2=4$. What are the orders $Q_2$ and $Q_3$?

To choose $(s,S)$, a simulation evaluates every pair on a grid, such as $s\in\{-5,\dots,15\}$ and $S\in\{-4,\dots,30\}$ with $s<S$, and keeps the pair with the lowest average cost. Why is the same demand list used for every pair?
options: So cost differences come from $(s,S)$, not the demands
Because the average cost does not depend on demand
So that every pair starts from the same position
So that every pair places the same number of orders

questions.question: A simulation evaluates every pair with $s\in\{-5,\dots,15\}$, $S\in\{-4,\dots,30\}$ and $s<S$ of an $(s,S)$ policy on one finite demand list and keeps the pair with the lowest average cost. What does the chosen pair guarantee?
options: The lowest average cost of any integer pair on that list
The lowest average cost among the grid pairs on that list
The lowest long-run expected cost for that kind of demand
The fewest orders among all the grid pairs on that list

questions.question: An $(s,S)$ policy with integers $s<S$ orders $S-P_{k-1}'$ at the start of period $k$ whenever the end-of-period inventory position $P_{k-1}'\le s$, and nothing otherwise. Demands are non-negative integers and the starting position satisfies $s<P_1\le S$. Let $P_k$ be the position at the start of period $k$, just after any order. Which is the smallest set of integers guaranteed to contain $P_k$ for every $k$ and every demand sequence?

An $(s,S)=(3,10)$ policy starts at inventory position $P_1=10$. Over periods $1$ to $10$ total demand is $31$, three orders are placed at the starts of periods $2$ to $10$, and period $10$ ends at position $6$. What is the total quantity ordered?

An $(s,S)$ policy with $s=3$ and $S=10$ starts at inventory position $P_1=14$, above $S$, and orders $S-P_{k-1}'$ at the start of period $k$ when the end-of-period position $P_{k-1}'\le s$. Demand is $4$ in every period. When is the first order placed, and how large is it?

Two $(s,S)$ pairs are simulated on one $10$-period demand list without backlog. Pair $(2,12)$ places $3$ orders and its start-of-period on-hand levels sum to $60$; pair $(2,5)$ places $7$ orders with sum $36$. Holding cost is $h=1$ per unit and setup cost $K$ per order. For which $K$ does $(2,12)$ cost less?

An $(s,S)$ policy orders $S-P'$ after an end-of-period inventory position $P'\le s$. A student claims that every order equals the total demand since the previous order, or since period $1$ for the first order. Which condition makes this true for every order, including the first?
options: The undershoot $s-P'$ is zero at every order

questions.question: Demand can take any non-negative real value, while $s$ and $S$ are integers. An $(s,S)$ policy with $s=S-1$ orders $S-P'$ after an end-of-period inventory position $P'\le S-1$; a base-stock policy with level $S$ orders $S-P'$ after every $P'<S$. Which statement about their orders is correct?
options: They always agree, because $s=S-1$ is the largest integer $s<S$
They differ, but only when one period's demand exceeds $S$
They differ when an end position lies strictly between $S-1$ and $S$
They always agree, because both policies order up to level $S$

questions.question: An unknown $(s,S)$ policy, ordering $S-P'$ when the end-of-period inventory position $P'\le s$ and nothing otherwise, is observed: after $P'=1$ it orders $9$, after $P'=4$ nothing, after $P'=3$ it orders $7$, and after $P'=-2$ it orders $12$. Which pair $(s,S)$ is it?

An $(s,S)=(2,8)$ policy starts at inventory position $P_1=8$ and orders $8-P'$ after an end-of-period position $P'\le2$. Demands are non-negative integers with total $25$ over periods $1$ to $10$. What is the largest possible number of orders placed at the starts of periods $2$ to $11$?
